title: U3 — Hierarchical Clustering
text:
1.1 Why hierarchical clustering?
K-means requires you to choose \(K\) before you start. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree (dendrogram) that shows the nested cluster structure at every level — you choose \(K\) after seeing the tree. It is also deterministic: the same data always gives the same result, unlike k-means.
A second advantage: the dendrogram reveals how clusters relate to each other. Are clusters 1 and 2 more similar to each other than to cluster 3? The tree shows this immediately.

title: U3 — Hierarchical Clustering
text:
1.2 Bottom-up (agglomerative) clustering
The most common approach:

Start with \(n\) clusters — every observation is its own cluster
Merge the two most similar clusters
Repeat until all observations are in one cluster

The result is a dendrogram. To get \(K\) clusters, cut the tree at height \(h\) such that exactly \(K\) branches extend below the cut.

title: U3 — Hierarchical Clustering
section: 1.3 Linkage — how similarity is measured between clusters
text:
1.3 Linkage — how similarity is measured between clusters
Once clusters contain multiple observations, we need to define distance between clusters (not just individual points).







Linkage
Distance between clusters A and B




Complete
Maximum distance between any point in A and any point in B


Single
Minimum distance (nearest neighbours)


Average
Average distance between all pairs


Ward’s
Increase in total WCSS when merging A and B



Ward’s linkage is usually recommended for health data — it produces compact, similarly sized clusters and connects directly to k-means (both minimise WCSS).

title: U3 — Hierarchical Clustering
text:
1.4 Reading a dendrogram

Height of a merge = dissimilarity at which two clusters joined
Long vertical lines = large gap between levels = natural cluster boundary
Short lines = clusters joined at similar dissimilarity = less clear separation
Cut the tree where you see the longest vertical lines before the cut

title: U1 — Principal Component Analysis
text:
1.1 You have seen this before
In STA220 you used factor analysis (FA) on the HAD scale — 14 items measuring depression and anxiety. FA found two latent factors: one loading on depression items, one on anxiety. Both factors were hidden dimensions that explained the correlations among items.
PCA asks a related but different question:









Factor Analysis (STA220)
PCA (STA230)




Goal
Find latent factors that cause correlations
Find directions that capture maximum variance


Model
\(\mathbf{X} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{f} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) (generative)
Geometric rotation of the data cloud


Output
Interpretable factors (depression, anxiety)
Principal components ordered by variance


Use case
Psychological measurement, construct validity
Compression, visualisation, multicollinearity



Both methods reduce many correlated variables to a smaller set of dimensions. PCA is simpler and makes no distributional assumptions — it is purely about variance.

title: U1 — Principal Component Analysis
text:
1.2 The geometry of PCA
Given \(n\) observations on \(p\) variables, PCA finds a sequence of orthogonal directions (principal components) \(\mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{z}_2, \ldots\) such that:
\[\mathbf{z}_1 = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}_1, \quad \text{where } \mathbf{v}_1 = \arg\max_{\|\mathbf{v}\|=1} \text{Var}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v})\]
Each subsequent component captures the maximum remaining variance, orthogonal to all previous ones.
In practice: standardise the variables (subtract mean, divide by SD), then compute the eigendecomposition of the covariance (or correlation) matrix:
\[\mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{D} \mathbf{V}^\top\]

\(\mathbf{V}\): eigenvectors = directions of principal components (loadings)
\(\mathbf{D}\): diagonal matrix of eigenvalues = variance explained by each component

Proportion of variance explained by component \(k\): \(\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j\)

title: U1 — Principal Component Analysis
text:
1.3 Reading PCA output







Output
What it tells you




Scree plot
Eigenvalues in decreasing order — look for an “elbow”


Loadings
How much each original variable contributes to each PC


Biplot
Observations (points) and variables (arrows) in PC space


Cumulative variance
How many PCs needed to explain e.g. 80% of variance

title: U1 — Principal Component Analysis
text:
1.4 Scaling matters
Always use scale = TRUE in prcomp(). Variables on different scales (age in years, cholesterol in mmol/L) would otherwise be dominated by whichever has the largest variance — purely an artefact of measurement units, not biology.

title: R4 — LASSO
text:
1.1 The LASSO objective
LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) uses an \(L_1\) penalty:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta})^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j| \right\}\]
The key difference from ridge: the \(L_1\) penalty produces sparse solutions — many \(\hat{\beta}_j = 0\) exactly. LASSO does variable selection automatically.

title: R4 — LASSO
text:
1.2 Why does L1 produce zeros?
Geometrically, the \(L_1\) constraint region (a diamond in 2D) has corners on the axes. The OLS ellipsoidal contours are likely to first touch one of these corners, where one or more \(\beta_j = 0\). The \(L_2\) constraint (a circle) has no corners, so the solution is rarely exactly zero.

text:

title: R4 — LASSO
text:
1.4 Elastic Net
The elastic net combines both penalties:
\[\lambda \left[\alpha \sum |\beta_j| + (1-\alpha) \sum \beta_j^2 \right]\]
With \(\alpha=1\) this is LASSO; \(\alpha=0\) is ridge. Elastic net handles correlated predictors better than pure LASSO. In glmnet(), alpha controls the mix.

title: R2 — Variable Selection
text:
1.1 Why not include everything?
Adding predictors always reduces training error but increases variance. With \(p\) predictors, OLS has \(p+1\) parameters to estimate. When \(p\) is large:

Variance of \(\hat{\beta}\) increases
Test MSE may be higher than a model with fewer predictors
Interpretation becomes harder

Variable selection finds the subset of predictors that minimises test error.

title: R2 — Variable Selection
text:
1.2 Best subset selection
Fit all \(2^p\) possible models, evaluate each by CV or an information criterion, pick the best. Exact but computationally infeasible for large \(p\) — for \(p=20\) there are over one million models.

title: R2 — Variable Selection
text:
1.3 Forward stepwise selection

Start with the null model (intercept only)
At each step, add the predictor that most improves fit
Stop when adding more predictors no longer helps (by CV or AIC)

Much faster than best subset (\(O(p^2)\) models), but not guaranteed to find the globally best subset.

title: R2 — Variable Selection
text:
1.4 Backward stepwise selection
Start with the full model, remove the least useful predictor at each step. Requires \(n > p\) to fit the full model.

title: R2 — Variable Selection
text:
1.5 Criteria for stopping








Criterion
Formula
Penalises




AIC
\(-2\ell + 2p\)
Predictive accuracy


BIC
\(-2\ell + p\log(n)\)
Harder penalty, simpler models


Adjusted R²
\(1 - \frac{\text{RSS}/(n-p-1)}{\text{TSS}/(n-1)}\)
Extra parameters


CV error
Estimated test MSE
Directly estimates generalisation

title: F2 — Bias-Variance Tradeoff
text:
1.1 Decomposing prediction error
For a fixed test point \(x_0\), the expected test MSE decomposes as:
\[\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[(y_0 - \hat{f}(x_0))^2\right]}_{\text{Expected test MSE}} = \underbrace{\left[\text{Bias}(\hat{f}(x_0))\right]^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\hat{f}(x_0))}_{\text{Variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2_\varepsilon}_{\text{Irreducible}}\]
where the expectation is over repeated training sets.








Component
Definition
Changes with complexity?




Bias²
How far \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x_0)]\) is from \(f(x_0)\)
Decreases as complexity increases


Variance
How much \(\hat{f}(x_0)\) varies across training sets
Increases as complexity increases


Irreducible
\(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) — noise floor
Fixed, never changes

title: F2 — Bias-Variance Tradeoff
section: 1.2 The U-shaped test error curve (ESL Figure 7.1)
text:
1.2 The U-shaped test error curve (ESL Figure 7.1)
This is the central figure of the course:

Training error (blue): monotonically decreasing — more complex models always fit the training data better
Test error (red): U-shaped — first decreases as we reduce bias, then increases as variance dominates
The minimum of the test error curve is the sweet spot: not too simple, not too complex







ImportantKey message



A model that fits the training data perfectly is not necessarily a good model. The goal is to generalise to new data — and that requires balancing bias against variance.

title: F2 — Bias-Variance Tradeoff
section: 1.3 Two approaches to finding the sweet spot
text:
1.3 Two approaches to finding the sweet spot

Analytical — penalise model complexity in the selection criterion (AIC, BIC, adjusted R²)
Data-driven (resampling) — directly estimate test error from data (cross-validation, train/test split)

Block 1 uses both. Cross-validation is covered in F5.

title: C6 — ROC Curve & AUC
text:
1.1 The confusion matrix
For binary classification with threshold \(c\): classify as positive if \(\hat{p} > c\).




Actual +
Actual −




Predicted +
TP
FP


Predicted −
FN
TN



Key metrics:
\[\text{Sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad \text{(true positive rate, recall)}\] \[\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP} \quad \text{(true negative rate)}\] \[\text{PPV (Precision)} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\]

title: C6 — ROC Curve & AUC
text:
1.2 The ROC curve
The Receiver Operating Characteristic curve plots sensitivity (TPR) vs 1−specificity (FPR) as the threshold \(c\) varies from 0 to 1.

Top-left corner (TPR=1, FPR=0): perfect classifier
Diagonal (TPR = FPR): random classifier
AUC (Area Under the Curve): probability that a randomly chosen positive example scores higher than a randomly chosen negative example — ranges 0.5 (random) to 1.0 (perfect)

title: C6 — ROC Curve & AUC
text:
1.3 Choosing a threshold
The optimal threshold depends on the cost asymmetry:

In occupational health: missing a worker at risk (FN) may be more costly than a false alarm (FP) → lower threshold → higher sensitivity
Rule: choose threshold that maximises \(\text{Sensitivity} + \text{Specificity} - 1\) (Youden’s J) or matches clinical cost-benefit

title: C6 — ROC Curve & AUC
text:
1.4 Discrimination vs calibration
These are two distinct, independent model properties:








Aspect
Question
Metrics




Discrimination
Can the model rank positives above negatives?
AUC / C-statistic, sensitivity, specificity


Calibration
Are the predicted probabilities accurate?
Calibration plot, Hosmer-Lemeshow, Brier score



A model can discriminate well but be poorly calibrated — e.g., it ranks workers correctly but systematically overestimates risk. For clinical and public health decision-making, both must be reported.

title: C6 — ROC Curve & AUC
text:
1.5 Calibration metrics
Calibration plot: Group predicted probabilities into deciles. Compare the mean predicted probability to the observed event rate in each group. Points on the diagonal = perfect calibration.
Hosmer-Lemeshow test: Chi-squared test for calibration across \(g\) groups (usually 10). Non-significant \(p\) value = no evidence of poor calibration. Note: the test has low power in small samples.
Brier score: Mean squared error of predicted probabilities.
\[\text{BS} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{p}_i - y_i)^2\]
Ranges 0 (perfect) to 1. For a balanced outcome, a random (0.5 always) classifier gives BS = 0.25.

title: C6 — ROC Curve & AUC
text:
1.6 Kappa statistic
Cohen’s kappa corrects accuracy for chance agreement:
\[\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}\]
where \(p_o\) is observed accuracy and \(p_e\) is accuracy expected by chance (based on marginal distributions). Interpretation: \(\kappa = 0\) means no better than chance; \(\kappa > 0.6\) is substantial agreement; \(\kappa > 0.8\) is almost perfect.






WarningImbalanced data and misleading accuracy



With 89% SWP=1 in the SWP dataset, always predicting SWP=1 achieves 89% accuracy — but \(\kappa = 0\). Accuracy is misleading when classes are imbalanced. Report AUC and sensitivity alongside accuracy, and always check kappa.

title: C6 — ROC Curve & AUC
section: 3.1 Calibration: are the predicted probabilities accurate?
text:
3.1 Calibration: are the predicted probabilities accurate?

# Decile-based calibration plot for logistic regression
cal_df <- data.frame(pred = p_logit, obs = test$SWP)
cal_df$decile <- as.integer(cut(rank(cal_df$pred), breaks = 10, labels = FALSE))
cal_sum <- cal_df |>
  dplyr::group_by(decile) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mean_pred = mean(pred),
                   mean_obs  = mean(obs),
                   n         = dplyr::n(),
                   .groups   = "drop")

ggplot(cal_sum, aes(mean_pred, mean_obs)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#888") +
  geom_line(colour = "#2980b9", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#2980b9", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 8), name = "n in decile") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Calibration plot — logistic regression (test data)",
       subtitle = "Dashed diagonal = perfect calibration; points should cluster on it",
       x = "Mean predicted probability (decile)",
       y = "Observed event rate (decile)") +
  theme_minimal()









# Brier score — mean squared error of predicted probabilities
brier <- mean((p_logit - test$SWP)^2)

# Kappa — corrects accuracy for chance agreement
pred_05 <- ifelse(p_logit > 0.5, 1, 0)
po <- mean(pred_05 == test$SWP)
pe <- mean(pred_05 == 0) * mean(test$SWP == 0) +
      mean(pred_05 == 1) * mean(test$SWP == 1)
kappa_val <- (po - pe) / (1 - pe)

title: C4 — Random Forests
text:
1.1 Bagging: reducing variance by averaging
A single tree has high variance. Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) reduces variance by averaging many trees:

Draw \(B\) bootstrap samples (size \(n\) with replacement) from training data
Fit a full tree on each bootstrap sample
Predict by majority vote across all \(B\) trees

Since each tree is trained on a different sample, averaging \(B\) uncorrelated trees reduces variance by factor \(B\) — while keeping bias approximately constant.

title: C4 — Random Forests
text:
1.2 Random forests: decorrelating trees
In bagging, if one predictor is very strong, most trees will use it at the top split — the trees are correlated. Averaging correlated trees reduces variance less effectively.
Random forests fix this by randomly selecting \(m\) predictors at each split (default: \(m = \sqrt{p}\) for classification). This decorrelates the trees and further reduces variance.

title: C4 — Random Forests
text:
1.4 Out-of-bag (OOB) error
Each tree is trained on ~63% of data (the bootstrap sample). The remaining ~37% (out-of-bag) can be used to estimate test error without a separate validation set. OOB error is a nearly unbiased estimate of test error.

title: C4 — Random Forests
text:
1.5 Variable importance and SHAP values
Variable importance in random forests = average decrease in Gini impurity from all splits on a variable, averaged across all trees. A high value means the variable is both frequently used and creates pure splits.
However, importance scores tell you which variables matter but not how they contribute for an individual observation. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) solves this.

1.5.1 The Shapley intuition
Imagine you want to attribute a predicted value to each predictor. For a model with age = 60 and BMI = 30 (and a bias of 50):



Predictors used
Prediction




{none}
50


{age=60}
70


{BMI=30}
85


{age=60, BMI=30}
100



The Shapley value for age averages its marginal contribution across all orderings:

Adding age first: \(70 - 50 = 20\)
Adding age after BMI: \(100 - 85 = 15\)
SHAP(age) \(= (20 + 15)/2 = 17.5\)

Unlike standardised regression coefficients (which are constant for every individual), SHAP values can differ for each observation — reflecting non-linear and interaction effects that trees capture naturally.






TipSHAP vs linear regression



In a linear model, the contribution of BMI is always \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{BMI}} \times \text{BMI}_i\) — a constant slope. With a random forest, SHAP might show a steep increase in contribution for very low BMI but a flat contribution in the normal range. This is the key advantage of tree-based SHAP over regression coefficients.

title: C2 — LDA & kNN
text:
1.1 Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
LDA models the class-conditional distributions \(P(\mathbf{X} \mid Y=k)\) as multivariate Gaussians with the same covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). Via Bayes’ theorem, this gives a linear decision boundary. QDA relaxes equal-covariance, giving a quadratic boundary but estimating more parameters.

title: C2 — LDA & kNN
text:
1.2 k-Nearest Neighbours (kNN)
kNN is non-parametric — no distributional assumption:

For a new point \(\mathbf{x}_0\), find the \(k\) closest training points
Assign the majority class among those neighbours

Small \(k\) = flexible, low bias, high variance. Large \(k\) = smooth, high bias, low variance. Optimal \(k\) found by cross-validation.

title: C1 — Logistic Regression
text:
1.1 From regression to classification
In classification the outcome \(Y\) is categorical. For binary \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\), we model the probability of belonging to class 1:
\[p(\mathbf{x}) = P(Y = 1 \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})\]
We then classify: \(\hat{Y} = 1\) if \(\hat{p}(\mathbf{x}) > 0.5\) (or another threshold).

title: C1 — Logistic Regression
text:
1.2 The logistic model
Logistic regression models \(p(\mathbf{x})\) via the logit link:
\[\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{1 - p(\mathbf{x})} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p\]
Equivalently:
\[p(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}}}{1 + e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\]
The coefficients \(e^{\beta_j}\) are odds ratios — the multiplicative change in odds of \(Y=1\) per unit increase in \(x_j\).

title: C1 — Logistic Regression
text:
1.3 Class imbalance
When one class is rare (e.g., only 11% have \(Y=0\) in SWP_CTW), a naive classifier that always predicts the majority class achieves high accuracy but is useless. Alternatives:

Use sensitivity and specificity instead of accuracy
Report AUC (area under the ROC curve)
Adjust the decision threshold away from 0.5
Resample: oversample the minority class (SMOTE) or undersample the majority

title: C3 — Decision Trees (CART)
text:
1.1 How CART works
A classification tree recursively splits the predictor space into rectangular regions. At each node, it finds the predictor \(X_j\) and split point \(s\) that minimises the Gini impurity in the resulting child nodes:
\[G = \sum_{k} \hat{p}_{mk}(1 - \hat{p}_{mk})\]
where \(\hat{p}_{mk}\) is the proportion of class \(k\) observations in region \(m\). \(G=0\) means a pure node (all one class); \(G=0.5\) is maximally impure for a binary outcome.

title: C3 — Decision Trees (CART)
text:
1.2 Pruning to avoid overfitting
A fully grown tree overfits — it memorises the training data. Cost-complexity pruning adds a penalty \(\alpha \cdot |\text{leaves}|\) to the tree size. The optimal \(\alpha\) is found by cross-validation.

title: C3 — Decision Trees (CART)
text:
1.3 Strengths and weaknesses







Strength
Weakness




Interpretable — easy to visualise
High variance — small data changes give different trees


Handles mixed variable types naturally
Usually outperformed by ensemble methods


Captures interactions automatically
Axis-aligned splits only


No need to standardise
Prone to overfitting without pruning

title: C5 — Boosting & XGBoost
text:
1.1 Boosting vs bagging
Bagging builds trees in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages. Boosting builds trees sequentially — each tree focuses on the mistakes of the previous ones.

title: C5 — Boosting & XGBoost
text:
1.2 Gradient boosting
At each step \(m\), fit a tree to the negative gradient of the loss function evaluated at the current predictions. For binary classification with log-loss:
\[\hat{f}^{(m)}(\mathbf{x}) = \hat{f}^{(m-1)}(\mathbf{x}) + \eta \cdot h_m(\mathbf{x})\]
where \(h_m\) is the new tree and \(\eta\) (learning rate) controls how much each tree contributes.

title: C5 — Boosting & XGBoost
text:

Parameter
Effect
Typical values




nrounds
Number of trees
100–1000 (with early stopping)


eta (learning rate)
Step size
0.01–0.3 — smaller = more robust

Tree depth
3–8 — shallower = less overfit

Fraction of rows per tree
0.5–1.0 — bagging-like regularisation

Fraction of columns per tree

Lower eta + more nrounds + early stopping = more robust. Start with eta=0.1, nrounds=500, use early stopping on validation set.

title: F1 — What is Statistical Learning?
text:
1.1 The statistical learning framework
We observe data \((x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\) and assume:
\[Y = f(\mathbf{X}) + \varepsilon\]
where \(f\) is the true unknown function we want to estimate, and \(\varepsilon\) is irreducible noise with \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\).
Statistical learning is the task of estimating \(\hat{f}\) from data, so that:
\[\hat{Y} = \hat{f}(\mathbf{X})\]
gives useful predictions for new observations.

title: F1 — What is Statistical Learning?
text:
1.2 Two goals: inference vs prediction








Goal
Question
Interpretability needed?




Inference
How does \(X_j\) affect \(Y\)?
Yes — coefficient meaning matters


Prediction
What is \(\hat{Y}\) for new \(X\)?
No — accuracy is the criterion



In STA230, we move toward prediction: we evaluate models by how well they perform on unseen data, not how well they fit the data they were trained on.

title: F1 — What is Statistical Learning?
text:
1.3 Supervised vs unsupervised

Supervised: we have both \(\mathbf{X}\) and \(Y\). Regression (continuous \(Y\)) or classification (categorical \(Y\)).
Unsupervised: no \(Y\). We look for structure in \(\mathbf{X}\) alone — clusters, principal components.

The course covers all three: supervised regression (Block 1), supervised classification (Block 2), unsupervised methods (Block 3).

title: F1 — What is Statistical Learning?
text:
1.4 The irreducible error
No matter how good \(\hat{f}\) is, we cannot reduce the prediction error below:
\[\text{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2_\varepsilon\]
This is the irreducible error — noise inherent in the data generating process. The reducible part is \(\mathbb{E}[(f(\mathbf{X}) - \hat{f}(\mathbf{X}))^2]\), which we can minimise by choosing \(\hat{f}\) well.

title: F3 — Training vs Test Error
text:
1.1 Optimism of training error
When we fit \(\hat{f}\) on training data and then evaluate on the same data, the estimate is optimistically biased. The model has already adapted to the specific noise in the training set.
The expected optimism is:
\[\text{Optimism} = \mathbb{E}[\text{Test MSE}] - \mathbb{E}[\text{Train MSE}] = \frac{2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Cov}(\hat{y}_i, y_i)\]
For OLS with \(p\) predictors: \(\text{Optimism} = 2p\sigma^2 / n\). This is why AIC and Mallow’s \(C_p\) add a penalty of \(2p\hat\sigma^2 / n\) to the training RSS.

title: F3 — Training vs Test Error
section: 1.2 Train/test split as the direct approach
text:
1.2 Train/test split as the direct approach
The simplest approach: split data once into training and test sets (e.g., 70/30). Fit on training, evaluate on test.
Advantage: Simple, unbiased estimate of test error.
Disadvantage: Wastes data; test MSE estimate has high variance (depends on which observations ended up in the test set).
Cross-validation (F5) improves on this by reusing all data.

title: F5 — Cross-Validation in Practice
text:
1.1 The one-standard-error rule
When selecting the best model via CV, the minimum CV error may not be the best choice. The 1-SE rule selects the simplest model whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum.
\[d^* = \min \{d : \text{CV}(d) \leq \text{CV}(d_{\min}) + \text{SE}(d_{\min})\}\]
This guards against selecting an unnecessarily complex model when a simpler one performs nearly as well.

title: F5 — Cross-Validation in Practice
text:
1.2 CV in glmnet: choosing λ
For ridge and LASSO regression, cv.glmnet() automates k-fold CV over a grid of \(\lambda\) values and returns:

lambda.min: the \(\lambda\) minimising CV error
lambda.1se: the largest \(\lambda\) within 1 SE of the minimum (more regularisation, simpler model)

In practice, lambda.1se is often preferred for parsimony.

title: F5 — Cross-Validation in Practice
text:
1.3 Pitfalls

Information leakage: never standardise predictors on all data before CV — standardise inside each fold
Nested CV: if you select both the model class and its hyperparameters, you need outer CV for honest evaluation
Classification: use stratified folds to preserve class proportions across folds

title: R1 — OLS Review & Diagnostics
text:
1.1 The OLS estimator
For \(Y = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\), OLS minimises the residual sum of squares:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\]
Properties (when assumptions hold):

Unbiased: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}] = \boldsymbol{\beta}\)
BLUE: Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (Gauss-Markov)
Variance: \(\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\)

title: R1 — OLS Review & Diagnostics
text:
1.2 When OLS struggles

\(p \approx n\)

\((\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})\) singular — OLS undefined

title: R1 — OLS Review & Diagnostics
text:

No high-leverage + high-residual outliers

title: R3 — Ridge Regression
text:
1.1 The ridge objective
Ridge regression adds an \(L_2\) penalty to the OLS loss:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta})^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2 \right\}\]
The penalty \(\lambda \sum \beta_j^2\) shrinks all coefficients toward zero. The tuning parameter \(\lambda \geq 0\) controls the amount of shrinkage:

\(\lambda = 0\): OLS (no shrinkage)
\(\lambda \to \infty\): all \(\hat{\beta}_j \to 0\)

title: R3 — Ridge Regression
text:
1.2 Closed-form solution
\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\text{ridge}} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\]
Adding \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) makes the matrix invertible even when \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is singular or near-singular — this is why ridge works when \(p \geq n\).

title: R3 — Ridge Regression
text:

Key insight: Ridge introduces bias but reduces variance. The optimal \(\lambda\) minimises test MSE — found via cross-validation.

title: R3 — Ridge Regression
text:
1.4 Important: standardise predictors
Ridge shrinks coefficients, but the amount of shrinkage depends on predictor scale. Always standardise predictors before applying ridge (and LASSO). glmnet() does this automatically by default.

title: R5 — Model Comparison & Workflow
text:
1.1 The complete regression workflow
1. Explore data          → distributions, missingness, outliers
2. Pre-process           → log-transform skewed outcomes, standardise predictors
3. Split data            → train (70%) / test (30%) — or use CV throughout
4. Fit candidate models  → OLS, forward stepwise, ridge, LASSO
5. Select model          → by CV RMSPE on training data only
6. Evaluate              → test RMSPE on held-out test set (once, at the end)
7. Report                → coefficients, CIs, test performance, clinical interpretation






WarningThe golden rule



The test set is used exactly once — at the end. If you look at the test set to make model choices, it is no longer a clean test set.

title: R5 — Model Comparison & Workflow
text:
1.2 Which method to choose?



Situation
Recommended method

\(p\) large, many small effects
Ridge

title: R5 — Model Comparison & Workflow
text:
1.3 Reporting test performance
Report RMSPE (or MAE) on the test set with a confidence interval:
\[\text{RMSPE} \pm 1.96 \times \frac{\text{SD of squared errors}}{\sqrt{n_{\text{test}}}}\]
Never report only training performance. Always compare to a baseline (e.g., predicting the mean: \(\text{RMSPE}_{\text{null}} = \text{SD}(Y)\)).

title: U2 — K-Means Clustering
section: 1.1 Supervised vs unsupervised — the key distinction
text:
1.1 Supervised vs unsupervised — the key distinction
In Blocks 1 and 2 you always had a response variable Y: SBP to predict, disease to classify. Clustering has no Y. You observe \(\mathbf{X}\) and ask: are there natural subgroups in this data?
In STA220 you asked a related question: do HAD items group into depression and anxiety? Factor analysis answered this by finding latent dimensions. Clustering answers a different version: do patients group into distinct health profiles? No labels are assumed — the groups emerge from the data geometry.

title: U2 — K-Means Clustering
text:
1.2 The k-means algorithm
Given \(n\) observations and a chosen number of clusters \(K\), k-means minimises the total within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS):
\[\text{WCSS} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{i \in C_k} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) is the centroid (mean) of cluster \(k\).
Algorithm (Lloyd’s):

Randomly initialise \(K\) centroids
Assign each observation to the nearest centroid
Update each centroid as the mean of its assigned observations
Repeat steps 2–3 until assignments stop changing

The algorithm converges to a local minimum — not necessarily the global minimum. Always run with multiple random starts (nstart in R) and take the best result.

title: U2 — K-Means Clustering
text:
1.3 Choosing K — the elbow method
Run k-means for \(K = 1, 2, \ldots, K_{\max}\) and plot WCSS against \(K\). WCSS always decreases as \(K\) increases (more clusters = smaller groups = tighter fit). Look for an elbow — the point where the rate of decrease slows sharply.
There is no objectively correct \(K\). Domain knowledge matters: do you expect 2 patient profiles or 5? The elbow is a heuristic, not a rule.

title: U2 — K-Means Clustering
text:
1.4 Important: scale your variables
K-means uses Euclidean distance. If Age is measured in years (range 20–80) and Cholesterol in mmol/L (range 2–8), Age will dominate purely because of its larger scale. Always standardise before clustering.
